title: Can Make Palindrome from Substring
statement:
You get a lowercase string `s` and a list `queries` in which every `queries[i]` is `[left, right, k]`. A query looks at the substring of `s` running from index `left` to index `right`, both ends included. You may shuffle that substring's letters into any order, and afterwards overwrite at most `k` of its positions, each with any lowercase letter of your choice (every position you overwrite costs one of the `k`).

Return a list of booleans whose `i`-th entry is `true` when query `i` can turn its substring into a palindrome this way, and `false` otherwise. Queries are independent: none of them changes `s`.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Because the letters can be shuffled, only how many times each letter appears matters. A palindrome can have at most one letter with an odd count (the one in the middle). One overwrite can fix two odd letters at once: change one copy of an odd letter into another odd letter, and both counts become even. So with `oddCount` odd letters the query needs `floor(oddCount / 2)` overwrites.

Counting letters for each query separately costs O(length) per query, which is too slow for 10^5 queries on a 10^5 string. Only the parity of each count matters, so a prefix of parity bitmasks answers each query in O(1) work.

## Approach

1. Build `prefix`, where bit `c` of `prefix[i]` says whether letter `c` appears an odd number of times in the first `i` letters. Each step XORs in the letter's `bit`.
2. For a query, `prefix[right + 1] ^ prefix[left]` gives the parity mask `odd` of the substring.
3. Count the set bits of `odd` into `oddCount` by clearing the lowest set bit until the mask is zero.
4. Push `floor(oddCount / 2) <= k` into `answer`.

## Example 1, step by step

With `a = 1`, `b = 2`, `c = 4`, `d = 8`, the string `"abcda"` gives `prefix = [0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 14]`.

- `[3, 3, 0]`: `15 ^ 7 = 8`, one odd letter, needs 0 overwrites: `true`.
- `[1, 2, 0]`: `7 ^ 1 = 6`, two odd letters, needs 1: `false`.
- `[0, 3, 1]`: `15 ^ 0 = 15`, four odd letters, needs 2: `false`.
- `[0, 3, 2]`: same mask, 2 overwrites allowed: `true`.
- `[0, 4, 1]`: `14 ^ 0 = 14`, three odd letters (`b`, `c`, `d`), needs 1: `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + q): one pass builds `prefix`, and each query clears at most 26 bits.
- Space: O(n) for `prefix` (plus the output list).

## Pitfalls

- The substring includes both ends, so use `prefix[right + 1]` with `prefix[left]`.
- Compare `floor(oddCount / 2)` with `k`, not `oddCount` itself: each overwrite fixes two odd letters, and one odd letter can stay in the middle.
- Recounting letters for every query works on small inputs but is O(n · q) and times out.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `prefix[i]` | parity bitmask of letter counts in `s[0..i-1]` |
| `bit` | the mask with only the current letter's bit set |
| `left`, `right`, `k` | the current query |
| `odd` | parity mask of the substring; it is cleared while counting |
| `oddCount` | number of letters with an odd count in the substring |
| `answer` | the results, one per query |

narration.2: prefix[i] will hold the odd/even pattern of letter counts in the first i letters; it starts all even.
narration.4: Turn the letter into a single bit: a is bit 0, b is bit 1, and so on.
narration.5: XOR flips that letter's parity, giving the pattern for one more letter.
narration.10: XOR of two prefixes cancels the shared part, leaving the parities of s[left..right].
narration.12: Keep going while some letter still has an odd count.
narration.13: Clear the lowest set bit of the mask.
narration.16: Each overwrite fixes two odd letters and one may stay in the middle, so floor(oddCount / 2) overwrites are needed.
